posts.title: PHP's Security Hangover Is Still WordPress's Crisis. Python Is the Way Out.
posts.intro: WordPress still runs more than a third of the web, on a language whose early design choices keep showing up in production. Here is a look at real PHP and WordPress vulnerabilities, and why Python frameworks are a safer default.
body: According to [W3Techs](https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/cm-wordpress) as of November 26, 2026, WordPress runs 38.4% of all websites, and 57.3% of sites whose content management system is known. The usual defense is that WordPress core is fairly well maintained, and that modern PHP 8 is a different language from the PHP of 2005. Both points are partly true, and both dodge the real problem: unsupported PHP versions, a plugin economy that produces thousands of new vulnerabilities a year, and a language that still makes the dangerous thing too easy unless you opt into discipline.

body.h2: PHP spent years teaching developers the wrong defaults

body: The official [PHP 5.4.0 release announcement](https://www.php.net/releases/5_4_0.php) listed what finally had to be ripped out: register globals, magic quotes, and safe mode. Register globals promoted request data into variables, making it easy to confuse attacker input with trusted state. Magic quotes escaped data automatically, and inconsistently. PHP's [manual](https://www.php.net/manual/en/security.variables.php) still cites both as convenience settings that obscured the origin and integrity of input and contributed to injection risks, removed only in PHP 5.4.0.

The [PHP 8.0 release announcement](https://www.php.net/releases/8.0/en.php) notes that in PHP 7, `0 == 'foobar'` evaluated to true — the kind of loose type juggling that has underpinned authentication bypasses for years. PHP 8 made that comparison false, and `match` uses strict comparisons, but those improvements arrived after a generation of WordPress plugin code had been written against the old rules. Strict types exist, yet as the [PHP manual](https://www.php.net/manual/en/security.variables.php) notes, you enable them with `declare(strict_types=1)`. Safety is still an opt-in.

The [docs for `unserialize()`](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.unserialize.php) warn not to pass it untrusted input, because unserialization can load and execute code through object instantiation and autoloading. With [`allow_url_include`](https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.remote-files.php) enabled, `include` and `require` can pull code from HTTP or FTP URLs.

In June 2024 came CVE-2024-4577, a critical PHP-CGI argument injection bug on Windows, scored 9.8 in the [official CVE record](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2024-4577). The PHP Group's [CVE description](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2024-4577) says that on Windows systems using certain code pages, "Best-Fit" character conversion can cause the PHP CGI module to treat attacker input as PHP options, revealing source code or running arbitrary PHP. [DEVCORE](https://devco.re/blog/2024/06/06/security-alert-cve-2024-4577-php-cgi-argument-injection-vulnerability-en/), which reported the issue, said it lets unauthenticated attackers bypass protections for CVE-2012-1823, a decade-old CGI flaw, and confirmed the attack on locales including Japanese (code page 932). [Akamai's Security Intelligence Response Team](https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/2024-php-exploit-cve-one-day-after-disclosure) later reported exploit attempts as early as one day after disclosure, including campaigns distributing Gh0st RAT, RedTail cryptominers, and XMRig.

body.h2: WordPress turns language risk into a planetary attack surface

body: WordPress core, to be fair, is not the main source of the bleeding. According to [Patchstack's State of WordPress Security in 2025 report](https://patchstack.com/whitepaper/state-of-wordpress-security-in-2025/), researchers found 7,966 new vulnerabilities in the WordPress ecosystem in 2024 — about 22 a day, and a 34% increase over 2023. Ninety-six percent were in plugins, 4% in themes, and only seven in WordPress core, none of which Patchstack described as a widespread threat. The core team deserves credit for that relative discipline. The ecosystem does not.

The same report found that 43% of the 2024 vulnerabilities required no authentication, and that 33% were not fixed in time for public disclosure, often in abandoned plugins that still had active installations. [Patchstack's 2024 vulnerability statistics](https://patchstack.com/database/statistics/wordpress/2024) put cross-site scripting at 47.69% of disclosed issues. Popularity was no shield: 1,018 vulnerabilities showed up in components with at least 100,000 installs.

In August 2024, Patchstack published an [advisory](https://patchstack.com/articles/critical-privilege-escalation-in-litespeed-cache-plugin-affecting-5-million-sites/) on CVE-2024-28000, an unauthenticated privilege-escalation flaw in LiteSpeed Cache, a plugin it described as having over five million active installations. A weak security hash in a user-simulation feature could let an unauthenticated visitor obtain administrator access; the vendor patched it in version 6.4. A year earlier, [CVE-2023-32243](https://patchstack.com/articles/critical-privilege-escalation-in-essential-addons-for-elementor-plugin-affecting-1-million-sites/) in Essential Addons for Elementor — over a million active installations, according to Patchstack — allowed any unauthenticated user to reset an administrator password. [Sucuri](https://blog.sucuri.net/2023/05/vulnerability-in-essential-addons-for-elementor-leads-to-mass-infection.html) later documented a mass-infection campaign: attackers tied to the Balada malware operation moved within 24 hours, and Sucuri's SiteCheck had already recorded over 6,000 detections.
That is the WordPress bargain. Plugins are cheap to ship and easy to stack, with no common security standard and no guarantee the author is still around. The attacker only needs one.

body.h2: The installed base will not move just because PHP got better

body: PHP 8 really did improve the language, with union types, saner string-to-number comparisons, consistent type errors, and tighter error handling. New PHP is a more serious language than the one that earned the old jokes. The web is not running it.

[WordPress.org's public PHP version statistics](https://wordpress.org/about/stats/), retrieved on November 25, 2026, show that just over 31% of WordPress sites are on a version that has already reached end of life, according to official dates published by [php.net](https://www.php.net/eol.php). PHP 8.1 reached end of life on December 31, 2025, and PHP 8.0 on November 26, 2023. PHP 7.4, unsupported since November 28, 2022, still accounts for about 14% of WordPress sites — nearly four years after official security support ended. [W3Techs](https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/pl-php) paints a similar picture for PHP as a whole: as of November 26, 2026, PHP is used by 67.9% of websites whose server-side language is known, and among those PHP sites, 23.7% are still on PHP 7, 7.1% on PHP 5, and 0.1% on PHP 4, all past end of life. When a bug like CVE-2024-4577 lands, sites on abandoned branches are already out of the official fix window.

body.h2: Python is not immune. Its defaults are simply less reckless.

body: Python will not save a careless team. The Python Package Index has been a target for supply-chain attacks, and [PyPI's own documentation](https://docs.pypi.org/about/security-and-internals/) is honest about it: in March 2024, a large typo-squatting campaign was serious enough that PyPI temporarily halted new user and project registrations.

The difference is what a modern Python framework gives you by default. [Django's official security documentation](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/security/) describes protections that are on from the start. Querysets are protected from SQL injection because queries are constructed with parameterization — the SQL and its parameters travel separately, and the database driver escapes the values. Templates automatically escape characters that would otherwise become cross-site scripting. CSRF protection is built into the framework, with middleware and template support, rather than a plugin you install after the first incident. Flask and FastAPI can be equally disciplined in smaller or API-first applications. If you need a CMS, Wagtail sits on Django and inherits those same defaults instead of asking you to assemble security from a directory of plugins.

You still have dependencies to update. What you do not have is a culture of installing someone else's PHP into production and hoping they patch faster than the scanners do. You write the application. You keep the surface area you chose.

body.h2: Choose the stack that does not fight you

body: None of this requires pretending that every WordPress site is doomed, or that PHP 8 programmers are careless. The evidence is plain: insecure defaults, a CMS that spread them across more than a third of the web, thousands of new plugin holes in a single year, and an installed base still stuck on unsupported runtimes.

If you are starting a site, or tired of plugin alerts, Python is the more grown-up choice. Django, Flask, FastAPI, and Wagtail will not eliminate risk, but they will stop asking you to earn security the hard way.

posts.title: A Practical Guide to Common Bash Commands for Server Management and Web Development
posts.intro: If you build or maintain websites, you will spend time in a terminal. This practical toolkit covers the everyday Bash commands that keep a server and a deploy running.
body: Bash is the default shell on most Linux servers, and a small set of commands covers most daily work: moving around the filesystem, checking a process, shipping a deploy, or reading a log when a site misbehaves. Each command below includes a short explanation and an example you can adapt.
**pwd** prints the current directory, which helps after you have jumped between project, backup, and system paths.
**cd** changes directory. Use `-` to return to the previous path, and `~` for your home directory.
**ls** lists files. These flags show hidden files, permissions, owners, and human-readable sizes.
**mkdir -p** creates a directory and any missing parent folders in one step.
**cp** copies files. `-r` copies a directory recursively. **mv** renames or moves a file or folder.
**cat** prints a file. For longer files, **less** lets you scroll and search without flooding the screen. Press `q` to quit.
Web servers often fail when a file has the wrong owner or permissions.
**ls -l** shows permissions, owner, and group.

**chmod** changes permissions. `755` is common for directories and scripts: the owner can read, write, and enter or execute; others can read and enter or execute. `644` is common for ordinary files: the owner can edit, and others can only read.
**chown** changes owner and group. On Ubuntu and Debian, the web server often runs as `www-data`. `-R` applies the change to a directory and its contents.
Avoid `chmod 777`. It makes a path world-writable and is almost never the right fix.
When a site is slow or a deploy appears stuck, check the machine before you change application code.
**ps** lists processes. Pipe it to **grep** to find one service.
**top** shows a live view of CPU and memory use. Press `q` to quit.

**kill** asks a process to exit. Use the PID from `ps` or `top`. The default signal is `SIGTERM` (`-15`), which lets the program clean up. `kill -9` sends `SIGKILL` and should be a last resort, because the process cannot shut down gracefully.
**df -h** reports disk space in a readable form. **free -h** shows memory, including swap.
Most server work happens over SSH.
**ssh** opens a remote shell. Add `-p` if the server does not use the default port 22.
**scp** copies files over SSH. `-r` copies a directory.

**rsync** is usually better for deploys and backups, because it copies only what changed. `-a` preserves permissions and timestamps, `-v` is verbose, and `-z` compresses data in transit. A trailing slash on the source matters: `public/` copies the contents, not the folder itself. `--dry-run` previews the transfer without writing files.
**curl** makes HTTP requests. `-I` fetches headers only, useful for checking a status code or redirect. `-o` saves the body to a file.
When something breaks, logs are usually faster than guesswork.
**tail -f** follows a file as new lines arrive. `-n` sets how much history to show first.
**grep** searches for a pattern. `-i` ignores case, `-r` walks a directory, and `-n` prints line numbers.
**journalctl** reads systemd logs. `-u` selects a service, `-f` follows new entries, `-n` limits the line count, and `--since` limits the time window.

body.pre:
journalctl -u nginx -n 100 --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -u nginx -f

body: On Debian and Ubuntu, **apt** installs software and **systemctl** controls services. Update the package index before you install anything.

body.pre:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx

body: **systemctl status** shows whether a service is running and prints recent log lines. **reload** picks up a new configuration without a full restart when the service supports it, which is often preferable for Nginx. **restart** stops and starts it. **enable** makes it start on boot.

body.pre:
systemctl status nginx
sudo systemctl reload nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx

body: If a restart fails, check `journalctl -u nginx` before you change more settings.
These commands show up constantly in deploys and project work.

**git** is how most teams move code. `status` shows what changed, `pull` fetches and merges from the remote, and `log --oneline` gives a compact history. Run `git status` on a server before you pull, so you do not overwrite uncommitted fixes.

body.pre:
git status
git pull
git log --oneline -n 10

body: **find** locates files by name, type, or age. `-mtime +30` means last modified more than 30 days ago.
**tar** packs and unpacks archives. `-c` creates, `-x` extracts, `-z` uses gzip, `-v` is verbose, and `-f` names the file. Put the archive name immediately after `-f`.

After a deploy, set permissions deliberately. This pattern makes directories enterable (`755`) and ordinary files readable but not executable (`644`). Then add execute permission only on scripts that need it.
A terminal does exactly what you type, including mistakes.

Be careful with **rm -rf**. It deletes recursively and without confirmation, and there is no undo. Never run it against `/`, against a path you have not checked with `pwd` and `ls`, or against a variable that might be empty. If `$DIR` is unset, `rm -rf "$DIR/"` can expand into a path you did not intend. Prefer a specific, fully written path, and consider moving a directory aside with `mv` before you delete anything on production.

Treat **sudo** as a multiplier. It can edit system files, restart services, and destroy data. Read the full command before you enter your password. If you use a shared deploy account, confirm you are on the right server with `hostname` and `pwd`.

Other habits that help: run `rsync --dry-run` before a real sync, avoid `chmod 777` and `chmod -R 777`, quote your variables, and do not paste a long command into production until you understand every flag.

You do not need hundreds of commands to manage a server well. You need a reliable handful for the filesystem, permissions, processes, SSH, logs, and deploys. Practice them on a development machine or a disposable VPS, then use them the same way in production: look first, change second, and keep a backup you can restore.
At Tenshi Systems Engineering, we build websites and software, and these are the kinds of commands we use when we ship, debug, and keep a site healthy after launch.

posts.title: AI for Small Business in Wisconsin: Practical Uses That Save Time
posts.intro: You do not need a data science team to get real value from AI. Here are practical, low-risk ways Wisconsin small businesses are using it today, and how to start without wasting money.
body: Artificial intelligence gets talked about as if it were only for tech giants. In practice, the most useful AI tools for a small business are modest: they answer routine questions, draft first versions of documents, and take repetitive steps off your plate. For a restaurant in Madison, a contractor in Green Bay or a clinic in Eau Claire, that can mean hours back every week.
This guide walks through the uses that tend to pay off first, what to watch out for, and a simple way to get started.

Most businesses answer the same handful of questions again and again: opening hours, prices, whether you serve a certain area, how to book. A well-configured chat assistant on your website can handle these at any hour, using only information you have approved, and hand anything unusual to a person.

The key is to keep it honest and narrow. A good assistant says when it does not know, never invents prices or promises, and makes it easy to reach a human. We cover the details in [AI chatbots for small business: what they can and cannot do](blog/ai-chatbots-for-small-business-what-they-can-and-cannot-do.html).

AI writing tools are good at first drafts: a follow-up email after a site visit, a product description, a social media post, a polite reply to a review. You stay the editor. Read every draft, correct the facts, and make it sound like you. Used this way, AI removes the blank page without removing your judgment.

Many small tasks follow the same pattern every time: copy a web form into a spreadsheet, send a confirmation, add a reminder to a calendar, file an invoice. Simple automation, sometimes with an AI step to read or summarize text, can link these together so they happen on their own.

ul: **Booking and scheduling:** confirmations and reminders sent automatically, fewer no-shows.
**Lead follow-up:** every inquiry from your website gets a prompt, personal reply and lands in one list.
**Paperwork:** receipts and documents sorted and summarized so nothing gets lost.

body.h2: 4. Making Sense of Your Own Data

body: If you have sales records, website analytics or customer feedback, AI tools can help you spot patterns: which services people ask about most, which pages lead to inquiries, which months are busiest. Treat the answers as a starting point for questions, not as final truth, and check anything important against the source.

ul: **Privacy:** do not paste customer personal information into tools that are not set up for it. Check what each service does with your data.
**Accuracy:** AI can sound confident and still be wrong. Keep a person responsible for anything sent to customers.
**Cost creep:** many tools charge per user or per use. Start small and measure whether it actually saves time.

body: Pick one task that is frequent, predictable and a little tedious. Try an AI-assisted version for a few weeks, measure the time it saves, and only then expand. Small, measured steps beat a big, expensive rollout.

posts.title: AI Chatbots for Small Business: What They Can and Cannot Do
posts.intro: A website chatbot can answer customers around the clock, or it can frustrate them and give wrong answers. Here is how to tell the difference before you add one to your site.
body: Modern AI chatbots can hold a natural conversation, which makes them tempting for any business that gets a steady stream of questions. Done well, a chatbot answers instantly, captures leads after hours and frees your staff for work that needs a person. Done badly, it gives confident wrong answers and drives customers away.

body.h2: What a Good Small Business Chatbot Does Well

ul: **Answers routine questions** about hours, services, service areas, parking, booking and policies, using information you have written and approved.
**Captures inquiries after hours** by collecting a name, contact details and a short description, then passing them to you.
**Points people to the right page,** such as your booking form, menu, price list or contact page.
**Speaks several languages,** which helps if your customers do not all prefer English.
**Invent prices, availability or promises.** If the answer is not in the information you gave it, it should say so and offer to connect the visitor with a person.
**Give medical, legal or financial advice.** Clinics, law offices and accountants need especially careful limits.
**Hide the human option.** Every chat should make it easy to call, email or request a callback.
**Collect more personal data than it needs.** Ask only for what you will actually use, and say how it will be handled.

body.h2: Questions to Ask Before You Add One

ul: Where does the chatbot get its answers, and can we control and update that information ourselves?
What happens when it does not know something?
Where are conversations stored, who can read them, and for how long?
How much does it cost as traffic grows?
Can we review conversations to see what customers are really asking?

body: After launch, read a sample of conversations every week at first. Look for wrong answers, questions it cannot handle and points where visitors give up. Those are your to-do list: update the information it uses, adjust its limits, or add a page to your website that answers the question properly for everyone.

posts.title: Local SEO for Wisconsin Small Businesses: A Plain-English Guide
posts.intro: When someone nearby searches for what you sell, you want to be one of the first names they see. Here is how local search works and the steps that matter most for a Wisconsin small business.
body: Local SEO is the work of showing up when people search for a business near them: "plumber in Madison", "bakery near me", "web design Milwaukee". These searches often come from people ready to call, visit or buy, which makes them some of the most valuable visitors a small business can get.
The good news is that most of the work is straightforward and within reach of any business owner. Here is where to focus.

body.h2: 1. Claim and Complete Your Google Business Profile

body: Your Google Business Profile is the listing that appears in Google Maps and in the box of local results. Claim it, verify it, and fill in everything: your exact business name, category, service area or address, hours, phone number, website, services and photos. Keep it updated when hours change, especially around holidays.

body.h2: 2. Keep Your Name, Address and Phone Consistent

body: Search engines compare your details across the web: your website, your profile, directories and social media. Use the same business name, address and phone number everywhere, written the same way. Inconsistent details make it harder for search engines to trust which information is correct.

ul: **Say where you work.** Mention your city and the areas you serve in plain words on your homepage and service pages.
**Give each main service its own page,** with a clear title and description that says what it is and where you offer it.
**Add your contact details** to every page, usually in the footer.
**Use structured data** (schema markup) so search engines can read your business name, location and services reliably.
**Make it fast and mobile-friendly.** Most local searches happen on phones.

body.h2: 4. Earn Reviews, and Reply to Them

body: Reviews influence both rankings and customers. Ask happy customers for a review shortly after a job, make it easy with a direct link, and reply to every review, good or bad, politely and briefly. Never buy reviews or offer rewards in exchange for positive ones; it breaks the platforms' rules and can get your listing penalized.

body.h2: 5. Get Listed Where Wisconsin Customers Look

body: Beyond Google, list your business on Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yelp and the directories that matter in your industry. Local organizations count too: your chamber of commerce, business associations and community groups often link to members, which helps both visibility and trust.

Articles that answer your customers' real questions, written with your area in mind, give search engines more reasons to show your site and give visitors more reasons to trust you. A short guide to seasonal maintenance in a Wisconsin winter, for example, is far more useful than a generic post.

Local SEO builds over weeks and months, not days. Use Google Search Console and your Business Profile insights to see which searches bring people in, and keep improving the pages and listings that matter most.

posts.title: Domain Names and Business Email: Getting Your Online Foundations Right
posts.intro: Your domain name and business email are some of the smallest line items in your budget, yet almost everything else online depends on them. Here is how to choose them well, keep them in your hands, and set them up so your messages arrive.
body: Before a customer sees your website, reads your email, or clicks a link you shared, a quiet system has already done its work. Your domain name, such as yourcompany.com, points people to the right place. Your email settings tell other mail systems that a message really came from you. When these foundations are set up carefully, nobody notices them. When they are not, you may face a website that suddenly disappears, invoices that land in spam, or a former contractor who still controls your company's name online.
This guide explains the essentials in plain English, so you can make good decisions or ask the right questions of whoever manages them for you.

body.h2: Choosing a Domain Name People Can Remember and Type

body: A good domain name is short, easy to say out loud, and easy to spell after hearing it once. Imagine telling it to someone over the phone. If you need to explain hyphens, unusual spellings, or numbers written as words, it will cost you visits and emails that never arrive.
A few practical guidelines:

ul: **Match your business name where you can.** If the exact name is taken, a short, natural addition, such as your city or your main service, usually works better than an awkward abbreviation.

**Choose the ending with your customers in mind.** A .com is widely recognized around the world. For a business serving customers in one country, that country's own ending (such as .us, .ca or .de) signals a local presence. Some country endings require a local address or a registered company, so check the rules before you buy.

**Consider registering close variations.** Common misspellings, or both .com and a country ending, can be redirected to your main site so visitors still find you and others cannot use them to imitate you.

**Check before you commit.** Search the name online and in trademark records to make sure you are not stepping on another company's brand, and check whether matching social media handles are available.

body.h2: Make Sure the Domain Is Registered to You

body: This is the single most important point in this article. A domain is registered to a named owner, called the registrant. Whoever is listed there, and whoever holds the login to the registrar account, effectively controls the address.

It is common for a web designer, an IT contractor, or a well-meaning employee to register a domain in their own name or on their own account, just to get things moving. Years later, when that relationship ends, the business can find it cannot change its website or email without that person's cooperation. Sorting this out can take time and stress at exactly the wrong moment.
To avoid this:

ul: **List your company as the registrant** and use a company email address you control as the contact, not a personal address.
**Keep the registrar login in a company-owned account**, ideally stored in a password manager, with more than one trusted person able to reach it.
**Give partners their own access** where the registrar allows it, rather than sharing your main password. Then you can remove their access when a project ends.
**Keep a simple record** of where the domain is registered, when it renews, and who has access.

body.h2: Protect It from Expiring or Being Taken

body: Domains are rented, not bought outright. They are registered for a period, often one year at a time, and must be renewed. If a renewal fails because a card expired or reminder emails went to an old address, your website and email can stop working. If the domain is not recovered in time, someone else may register it.
A few settings reduce that risk considerably:

ul: **Turn on auto-renew** and keep the payment card up to date. Many registrars also let you renew for several years at once.
**Turn on two-factor authentication** for the registrar account. Anyone who gets into that account can redirect your website and email.
**Enable the registrar lock**, often called transfer lock, so the domain cannot be moved to another registrar without your deliberate action.
**Use privacy protection where available** so your personal details are not published in public domain records. Availability depends on the domain ending and the registrar.

body.h2: Why Business Email Should Use Your Own Domain

body: An address like info@yourcompany.com tells customers they are dealing with an established business. A free webmail address can feel less trustworthy, especially when you are sending quotes or invoices. Your own domain also means your email address stays the same if you change providers, and when staff leave, their mailbox belongs to the company, not to them.

Most small businesses use a hosted email service rather than running their own mail server. The well-known options include business plans from large providers, and many hosting companies bundle email as well. When comparing them, look at storage, security features such as two-factor authentication, how easily you can add and remove staff, shared mailboxes for addresses like sales@ or support@, and the quality of the calendar and mobile apps your team will use every day.

body.h2: Help Your Email Reach the Inbox: SPF, DKIM and DMARC

body: Email was designed decades ago without strong proof of who sent a message. That is why scammers can send messages that appear to come from your domain. Three settings, added to your domain's DNS records, help receiving mail systems check that a message really came from you:

ul: **SPF** lists the services that are allowed to send email for your domain, such as your email provider and your newsletter tool.
**DKIM** adds a digital signature to each message, so the receiving system can confirm it was not altered and was sent by an authorized service.
**DMARC** tells receiving systems what to do when a message fails those checks, such as deliver it, send it to spam, or reject it, and can send you reports about who is sending mail using your name.

body: Major mailbox providers increasingly expect these to be in place. Google's published email sender guidelines, for example, ask senders to set up SPF or DKIM, and require SPF, DKIM and DMARC for senders who send large volumes to Gmail addresses. Even if you send only a few messages a day, these settings help protect your reputation and make it harder for others to impersonate you.

A sensible approach is to start DMARC in a monitoring-only mode, review the reports to confirm that every legitimate service you use, including invoicing, booking and marketing tools, is set up correctly, and then tighten the policy step by step. Tightening too quickly can block your own legitimate messages, so this is worth doing carefully.

DNS records are the instructions that connect your domain to your website, your email and other services. Over the years, they tend to collect leftovers from old websites, tools you no longer use, and verification codes nobody remembers adding. Every so often, review them with someone who understands them. Remove what is no longer needed, document what remains, and before moving your website or email to a new provider, plan the change so nothing goes offline in between.

ul: Is the domain registered in the company's name, on an account the company controls?
Are auto-renew, two-factor authentication and the registrar lock turned on?
Do you know when the domain renews and who can access the account?
Does your team use email addresses on your own domain?
Are SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up for every service that sends email for you?
Has anyone reviewed your DNS records in the past year?

body: If you answered no or not sure to any of these, it is worth an hour of attention now. These foundations are inexpensive to set up properly and far more costly to repair in a hurry.

posts.title: Choosing Web Hosting for Your Business: A Plain-English Guide
posts.intro: Hosting is the part of your website most owners never see, until something goes wrong. Here is how the main options differ and what to ask before you choose.
body: Every website lives on a computer somewhere, connected to the internet around the clock. Web hosting is the service that provides that computer, keeps it running, and delivers your pages to visitors when they type in your address. It is easy to treat hosting as a commodity and pick the cheapest plan on offer. But the host you choose affects how fast your site loads, how often it is unavailable, how safe it is, and how much work it takes to keep it healthy.
This guide explains the main types of hosting in plain English, what actually matters when comparing them, and the questions worth asking before you sign up or move.
Most hosting falls into a handful of categories. The names vary from provider to provider, but the underlying ideas are consistent.

ul: **Shared hosting.** Your site sits on a server alongside many other websites, sharing its processing power, memory, and storage. It is inexpensive and usually comes with a simple control panel. The trade-off is that a busy or badly behaved neighbor can slow your site down, and you have limited control over the server's setup.

**Virtual private server (VPS).** One physical machine is divided into several isolated virtual servers, and you get one of them with a guaranteed share of resources. That brings more consistent performance and more control, but someone has to configure, update, and secure that server.

**Cloud hosting.** Your site runs on infrastructure spread across many machines run by a large provider. Resources can usually be added or reduced as needed, which suits sites with uneven traffic or growing applications. Pricing is often based on usage, which is flexible but can be harder to predict.

**Managed hosting.** This describes who does the work rather than the technology underneath. With a managed plan, the provider or your agency handles updates, backups, security, and monitoring. It costs more than doing it yourself, but it buys back time and reduces the risk of a forgotten update.

**Static site hosting.** If your site is built as pre-generated pages rather than pages assembled by a database on every visit, it can be served from simple, fast, and often low-cost platforms, frequently backed by a content delivery network. There is less software running, which also means less to break and less to attack.

body: There is no single best option. A five-page company site, an online shop, and a customer portal have very different needs.

body.h2: What Actually Matters When Comparing Hosts

body: Hosting plans are often marketed with long lists of features. A few factors matter far more than the rest.

ul: **Speed and location.** The physical distance between the server and your visitors affects how quickly pages arrive. If most of your customers are in one region, a server or content delivery network with a presence nearby will generally serve them faster than one on another continent. If you serve customers worldwide, a content delivery network that copies your files to locations around the globe helps everyone.
**Reliability.** Ask what uptime the provider commits to, what happens if it misses that commitment, and how outages are communicated. A status page and a clear history of incidents are good signs.

**Security.** Look for automatic HTTPS certificates, regular software patching, firewall protection, and isolation between customers. Find out who is responsible for updating your content management system and plugins, because hosts often secure the server but leave the application to you.

**Backups.** Confirm how often backups are taken, how long they are kept, where they are stored, and how quickly a site can be restored. A backup you have never tested restoring is a hope, not a plan.
**Support.** When something breaks, you want a knowledgeable person who responds promptly in a language you are comfortable with. Check the support channels and hours before you need them.
**Room to grow.** Consider whether you can upgrade resources, add a staging site for testing changes, or move to a larger plan without rebuilding everything.

body: The monthly price is only part of the picture. Introductory discounts often end after the first term, and renewal rates can be noticeably higher. Some plans charge separately for backups, email, SSL certificates, or extra storage. Cheaper plans may also cost you in other ways: slower pages that frustrate visitors, time spent applying updates yourself, or a stressful weekend recovering from an outage with no recent backup.
A fair comparison looks at the total cost over two or three years, including renewals and add-ons, alongside the time and risk each option involves.
Whatever you choose, make sure your business stays in control of its own assets. That means:

ul: **Registering your domain name in your company's name,** with login details your business holds, even if an agency manages it for you.
**Knowing where your site files and database live** and being able to get a full copy of them.
**Keeping a record of key accounts,** such as the domain registrar, hosting provider, and DNS settings, stored securely and shared with more than one trusted person.
**Separating email from web hosting where sensible,** so a problem with one does not take down the other.

body: These steps make it far easier to change providers or agencies later without losing your website or your email address.

body.h2: Questions to Ask Before You Choose

body: Before you sign up, or if you are reviewing your current setup, these questions will tell you a lot:

ul: Where are your servers located, and do you use a content delivery network?
What uptime do you commit to, and how do you notify customers of problems?
How often are backups taken, and how do I restore one?
Who is responsible for software updates and security patches?
What does the plan cost at renewal, and what costs extra?
How do I get my files and data out if I decide to leave?

body: If a provider cannot answer these clearly, that is useful information in itself.

Changing hosts is worth considering if your site is regularly slow, goes down without explanation, has been compromised, or has outgrown its plan. A careful migration copies everything to the new host, tests it thoroughly, and only then switches your domain over, ideally at a quiet time, so visitors never notice. Rushed moves are where email stops working or pages go missing, so it pays to plan.
Hosting rarely gets attention when it works well, and that is exactly the goal. The right choice is one that keeps your site fast, secure, and available, without demanding your time.

posts.title: Website Analytics in Plain English: How to Tell If Your Site Is Doing Its Job
posts.intro: A website can look fine and still miss its purpose. Here is how to read the numbers that show whether visitors find you, understand you, and get in touch.
body: A website can look professional, load quickly, and still fall short of the job that matters: helping the right people understand what you offer and take the next step. Analytics will not fix that on its own, but it will show you what is actually happening, instead of what you hope is happening. This guide explains the idea in plain English, names the numbers that usually matter, and suggests a simple monthly habit you can keep.

body.h2: Analytics Is a Record of Behavior, Not a Scorecard

body: Website analytics is a record of how people find your site and what they do while they are there. Typical tools show how many visits you received, which pages were opened, whether someone arrived from a search engine or a link, and whether they used a phone or a computer.

That record is useful, but it is not a verdict on your brand, and it is not a sales report. Think of it as a flashlight: it helps you see patterns, not a crystal ball. One well-installed tool, a few clear goals, and a regular look at the results are enough for most small and mid-size businesses.

Begin with questions you already have, not with a dashboard full of charts. Are people finding us? Which pages do they read? Do they get as far as contacting us? If a report does not help you answer those questions, you can usually ignore it, including vanity metrics such as raw page-view counts or follower totals that never turn into inquiries.

Look at trends over weeks and months, not a quiet Tuesday. The useful question is whether this month looks meaningfully different from last month, or from the same period last year if you have the data.

Pay attention to sources: search, direct visits (someone typing your address or using a bookmark), links from other sites, and social media. If almost all of your inquiries come from search, that is a clue about where to invest your energy. If a partner site sends visits that never contact you, the traffic may be the wrong audience, or the landing page may be unclear.

See which pages do the work. Service pages, a contact page, or a clearly written about page often matter more than the homepage. Notice which pages people open most often, and which ones they are on before they leave or get in touch.

Most important, measure whether people take the next step. In analytics tools this is often called a conversion, a goal, or a key event. For many companies that step is an inquiry form, a click on an email address or phone number, or a booking. A simple method is to send people to a thank-you page after they submit a form, and to count visits to that page. One to three goals is plenty. If most visitors use a phone, treat the mobile experience as the main one, not an afterthought.

A word of caution about bounce rate. It tries to show how often someone viewed a single page and left. That can be a problem on a service page that should lead to an inquiry, and perfectly normal on a page that answers one question quickly, such as your opening hours. Do not treat it as a single grade for the whole site.

body.h2: Set It Up So You Will Actually Use It

body: A complicated setup that nobody opens is worse than a simple one you review. Choose one analytics tool and install it correctly on every page, including the thank-you page if you have one. Popular options include Google Analytics and a number of privacy-focused alternatives; pick the one you will actually look at. Then define one to three goals that match real business outcomes, such as a completed inquiry, and decide who reviews the reports, and when.

Because analytics records information about visitors, treat it with the same care you would give any other customer data. Collect only what you need, be open about the fact that you use it, and follow the privacy rules that apply to your customers. In the United States several states have their own privacy laws, Europe has the GDPR, and other countries have their own requirements. This is not legal advice, but it is a reason to be conservative and clear.

A few habits often lead to confusion. More visits are not automatically better; a smaller number of people who get in touch is more valuable than a crowd that arrives and leaves. A change from four inquiries to six in a week is not yet a trend, so give decisions enough time and enough visits to be meaningful. If you rewrite a page, change the menu, and launch a promotion in the same week, you will not know what caused a rise or a drop. When a number jumps, look for a cause before you celebrate or panic.

The point of measurement is to improve something: a confusing headline, a buried contact link, a slow page, or a service description that does not answer the questions people actually have. Numbers that never lead to a change are just decoration.

body.h2: A Monthly Review You Can Keep

body: You do not need to watch your analytics every morning. Once a month, set aside half an hour and write down brief answers to five questions:

ul: Did overall visits rise, fall, or stay about the same compared with last month?
Where did useful visits come from?
Which pages were most used, and did any important page suddenly drop?
How many people completed the action you care about, such as an inquiry?
What is the one improvement we will try next month?

body: Keep those notes. Over a few months you will see patterns a single screenshot cannot show, which is useful when you brief a designer or developer. Launch day is only the beginning. Analytics is how you keep learning after the site is live, so each change has a reason and a way to tell whether it helped.

posts.title: Mobile-First Design: Why Your Website Should Start on the Smallest Screen
posts.intro: Many of your customers will meet your business for the first time on a phone. They might be on a train, standing in line, or comparing options on the couch. If your website was designed for a large desktop monitor and then squeezed down to fit a phone, they will feel it: tiny text, buttons that are hard to tap, and menus that fight back. Mobile-first design flips that process around. In this post, we explain what mobile-first and responsive design actually mean, why they matter for small and mid-size businesses, and how to check whether your own site measures up.

body.h2: Responsive Design and Mobile-First: What Is the Difference?

body: These two terms are often used together, but they describe different ideas.

ul: **Responsive design** means a single website adapts its layout to the screen it is viewed on. Columns stack, images resize, and navigation changes shape, all from the same code and the same web address.
**Mobile-first** is a way of working. Designers and developers plan the small-screen experience first, then add layout and features as more space becomes available.

body: The order matters. When you start with a large screen, it is easy to fill space with extras that later have to be hidden or crammed onto a phone. When you start small, you are forced to decide what is truly important, and that clarity usually improves the desktop version too.

body.h2: Why Mobile-First Matters for Your Business

body: A mobile-first approach is not just a technical preference. It affects how customers experience your brand and how search engines evaluate your site.

ul: **Search visibility:** Google uses mobile-first indexing, which means it primarily looks at the mobile version of your pages when deciding how to rank them. Content that is missing or broken on mobile can hurt you everywhere.
**First impressions:** A visitor who struggles to read your pricing or find your phone number on a phone may simply leave and try a competitor.
**Speed:** Designing for phones encourages lighter pages, which load faster on mobile networks and benefit every visitor.
**Focus:** Limited space pushes you to put your most important message and your main call to action front and center.

body.h2: The Core Principles of Mobile-First Design

body: Good mobile design follows a handful of practical rules. You do not need to be a designer to understand them.

ol: **Prioritize content.** Decide the one or two things a visitor must see on each page and put them near the top. Everything else supports those goals.

**Design for thumbs.** Buttons and links should be large enough to tap comfortably and spaced so people do not hit the wrong one. A common guideline is a touch target of roughly 44 to 48 pixels square.
**Keep text readable.** Body text should be large enough to read without zooming, typically around 16 pixels, with comfortable line spacing.
**Simplify navigation.** A short, clearly labeled menu works better than a long list of links. Put the most-used pages first.
**Use flexible layouts.** Content should flow into a single column on small screens and expand into multiple columns as space allows, using CSS techniques such as flexbox and grid.
**Optimize media.** Serve appropriately sized images to each device so phones are not downloading files meant for large monitors.

body: Even well-designed websites sometimes slip on the details. Watch for these frequent problems:

ul: Pop-ups that cover the entire screen and are difficult to close on a phone
Phone numbers and addresses that are not tappable
Wide tables or images that force sideways scrolling
Forms with tiny fields or the wrong keyboard type, such as a text keyboard for a phone number
Important information hidden inside images, where it cannot scale or be read by search engines
Hover-only menus or effects that do nothing on a touchscreen

body: Each of these creates friction, and friction is often what turns an interested visitor into a lost one.

body.h2: How to Test Your Website on Mobile

body: You can learn a lot about your site in about fifteen minutes. Try the following:

ol: **Use your own phone.** Visit your homepage and try to complete a key task, such as finding your hours or sending an inquiry. Note anything that feels slow or awkward.
**Try different devices.** Ask a colleague with a different phone or a tablet to do the same. Screens vary more than most people expect.
**Use browser developer tools.** Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all include a device mode that lets you preview your site at many screen sizes from your computer.
**Run Lighthouse.** Built into Chrome's developer tools, Lighthouse reports on performance, accessibility, and best practices, including several mobile-specific issues.
**Check real conditions.** Test on a mobile connection rather than office Wi-Fi to see how your site performs for people on the go.

body: Write down what you find. A simple list of problems, ordered by how much they affect customers, is a great starting point for improvements.

If you are planning a new website or a redesign, ask your design and development team how they approach mobile. Look for wireframes or mockups of the phone layout early in the process, not as an afterthought. Ask how images will be optimized, how navigation will work on small screens, and how the site will be tested across devices before launch. It is also worth asking who will maintain the site afterward, because new content added carelessly, such as oversized photos or wide tables, can quietly undo good mobile work over time.
Mobile-first design is ultimately about respect for your visitors' time and attention. When your site is easy to use on the smallest screen, it tends to be easier to use everywhere.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals Explained: A Plain-English Guide for Business Owners
posts.intro: "Your site is slow" is useful feedback, but it is not very specific. Slow to appear? Slow to respond when someone taps a button? Or does it simply feel unstable, with content jumping around as it loads? Google's Core Web Vitals give each of those frustrations a name and a measurable target. Understanding them helps you set clear goals and spend your improvement budget where it matters.
body: This guide explains each metric, what causes poor scores, and how to check your own site.

Core Web Vitals are a small set of measurements that Google uses to describe the real-world experience of loading and using a web page. They are part of what Google calls page experience signals, which it considers alongside many other factors, most importantly the relevance and quality of your content.
There are currently three Core Web Vitals:

rows: Loading: how quickly the main content appears
Responsiveness: how quickly the page reacts to taps, clicks, and key presses
Visual stability: how much content moves around unexpectedly

body: Google evaluates these at the 75th percentile of visits. In plain terms, a page passes when at least three out of four visits meet the target. So your score reflects visitors on older phones and slower connections, not just the fast laptop in your office.
INP replaced an older metric, First Input Delay, in March 2024. If you see FID in an older report, know that it is no longer part of the set.

body.h2: Largest Contentful Paint: "Is It Here Yet?"

body: LCP marks the moment the largest visible element, usually a hero image, a video poster, or a large block of headline text, finishes rendering. It is a good stand-in for when a visitor feels the page has arrived.
Common causes of a slow LCP include:

ul: Large, uncompressed hero images, especially photos uploaded straight from a camera
Slow server response times, often from underpowered hosting or no caching
Render-blocking CSS and JavaScript that must download before anything appears
Web fonts that delay text from showing
Main images loaded late because they are inserted by JavaScript or marked for lazy loading

body: Fixes usually start with the image itself: resize it to its displayed dimensions, convert it to a modern format such as WebP or AVIF, and tell the browser to prioritize it. Then look at hosting, caching, and a content delivery network (CDN).

body.h2: Interaction to Next Paint: "Did It Hear Me?"

body: INP looks at the interactions a visitor makes during their time on a page and reports one of the slowest. If someone taps "Add to cart" and nothing visibly happens for half a second, they may tap again, give up, or lose trust.
Poor INP is almost always about JavaScript. When the browser's main thread is busy running scripts, it cannot respond to the visitor. Typical culprits are:

ul: Too many third-party scripts, such as chat widgets, ad tags, heatmaps, and social embeds
Large JavaScript bundles from themes or page builders that load features you never use
Heavy work triggered by a single click, such as re-rendering a whole page to update one number

body: Improving INP often means auditing scripts and asking of each one: is this earning its place? Removing or delaying non-essential tools and breaking long tasks into smaller pieces can make a site feel noticeably more responsive.

body.h2: Cumulative Layout Shift: "Why Did That Move?"

body: You have probably tried to tap a link just as a banner loaded above it and pushed it away. CLS measures that kind of unexpected movement.
The usual causes are straightforward:

ol: Images and videos without set width and height, so the browser does not know how much space to reserve
Ads, embeds, or cookie banners injected above existing content
Web fonts that swap in and change the size of text after it first appears
Content added dynamically, such as a "free shipping" bar that appears a moment after load

body: The fix is to reserve space in advance: give media explicit dimensions, place banners in fixed slots, and choose font settings that minimize reflow. CLS is often the easiest of the three to improve.

body.h2: How to Check Your Own Scores

body: You do not need special software to get started. Two free tools from Google will tell you most of what you need to know.

ul: **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev): Enter any URL to see field data from real Chrome users, when enough data exists, plus lab data from a simulated test with specific recommendations.

**Google Search Console:** The Core Web Vitals report groups your pages into "Good," "Needs improvement," and "Poor," separately for mobile and desktop. It is the best way to see patterns across a whole site.

body: It helps to understand the difference between the two types of data. **Field data** comes from real visitors over the previous 28 days, so improvements take time to show up. **Lab data** comes from a single controlled test, which is useful for diagnosing problems and checking fixes immediately, but may not match what real visitors experience.
If your results show problems, resist the urge to chase a perfect score on every page. Instead:

ol: **Start with your most important templates.** Homepage, service pages, product pages, and contact page usually matter most.
**Fix by template, not by page.** On most sites, pages share layouts, so one fix to a template can improve hundreds of URLs.
**Prioritize mobile.** Mobile scores tend to be worse and mobile visitors are often your largest group.
**Measure before and after.** Record your baseline so you can confirm each change actually helped.
**Watch for regressions.** New plugins, tracking tags, and large images added later are the most common reasons good scores slip.

body: Remember that Core Web Vitals are a means to an end. The goal is not a green number in a report; it is a website that feels fast, responsive, and dependable to the people who use it.

[Request a consultation](contact.html#contact) and we will review your results, explain what they mean, and outline a practical plan to improve them.

posts.title: Web Accessibility Basics: What WCAG Means for Your Business Website
posts.intro: Imagine a customer who wants to book your service but cannot see the screen and relies on software that reads it aloud. Or someone with a tremor who navigates with a keyboard instead of a mouse. Or an older visitor who simply needs larger, higher-contrast text. If your website works for them, it is accessible. If it does not, you are turning away people who want to do business with you, often without ever knowing it.
body: Accessibility can sound like a technical specialty, but its foundations are surprisingly practical. This post explains the standard most of the world uses, why it matters for every business, and what you can check on your own site this week.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, or WCAG, are published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), the organization that develops many core web standards. The current version is WCAG 2.2, released in October 2023. The guidelines are organized into three conformance levels:

ul: **Level A:** The minimum. Failing these makes content unusable for some people.
**Level AA:** The level most organizations and many laws aim for. It covers the barriers that affect the largest number of users.
**Level AAA:** The highest level, often not achievable for every type of content, and usually applied selectively.

body: For most business websites, Level AA is the sensible target.

In the United States, the Americans with Disabilities Act is widely applied to business websites, and WCAG is the usual measure. Many other countries have their own accessibility rules as well. A website built to WCAG AA puts you on solid ground almost everywhere.

body.h2: The Four Principles, in Plain English

body: Every WCAG guideline falls under four principles, often remembered by the acronym POUR. Thinking in these terms makes the whole subject easier to grasp.
People must be able to take in the information, whether by sight, sound, or touch. This means:

ul: Providing text alternatives (alt text) for meaningful images
Offering captions for videos and transcripts for audio
Ensuring enough color contrast between text and background. WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text
Never relying on color alone to convey meaning, such as marking required fields only in red

body: People must be able to use the interface. Key requirements include:

ul: Every function works with a keyboard alone, not just a mouse
A visible focus indicator shows where you are on the page as you press Tab
Nothing flashes rapidly enough to trigger seizures
Users have enough time to read and complete tasks, or can extend time limits
Touch targets are large enough to activate reliably

body: Content and controls must make sense. That means clear language, predictable navigation that stays consistent from page to page, form fields with visible labels, and error messages that explain what went wrong and how to fix it.

Content must work with a wide range of browsers and assistive technologies, now and in the future. In practice, this comes down to clean, standards-based code: proper headings, real buttons and links instead of clickable boxes, and correct use of HTML elements so screen readers can interpret the page.
Accessibility is the right thing to do, and it also benefits your business in concrete ways.

ol: **You reach more customers.** People with disabilities, aging customers, and people with temporary injuries all use the web.
**Everyone gets a better experience.** Captions help people watching in a quiet office. Good contrast helps anyone reading outdoors in sunlight. Clear forms reduce errors for all users.
**Search engines benefit too.** Descriptive headings, alt text, and well-structured pages help search engines understand your content.
**You reduce legal and reputational risk.** Addressing accessibility proactively is far easier than responding to a complaint.

body: You do not need to be an expert to spot many common problems. Try these checks on your homepage and your most important form:

ul: **Unplug your mouse.** Use Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and the arrow keys to move through the page. Can you reach every link and button? Can you always see where you are?
**Zoom to 200 percent.** Does the text remain readable without overlapping or forcing sideways scrolling?
**Check your images.** Do meaningful images have descriptive alt text? Decorative images should have empty alt text so screen readers skip them.
**Look at your headings.** Is there one main heading (H1), followed by a logical order of subheadings? Headings should reflect structure, not just make text bigger.
**Test your contrast.** Free tools such as the WebAIM Contrast Checker will tell you whether your text colors meet the standard.
**Submit a form with mistakes.** Are errors explained in text, near the field, in a way that would make sense without color?
**Run an automated scan.** Tools such as Lighthouse in Chrome or the WAVE browser extension flag many issues quickly.

body: A word of caution: automated tools are useful but catch only a portion of accessibility problems. Many issues, like whether alt text is actually meaningful or whether a process makes sense, require human judgment. Testing with a real screen reader, such as VoiceOver on Apple devices or NVDA on Windows, reveals a great deal.

body.h2: Making Accessibility Part of Your Process

body: The most cost-effective time to address accessibility is at the beginning. When designers choose colors, they can check contrast immediately. When developers build components, they can use proper HTML from the start. When content writers add images, they can write alt text as they go.

For an existing website, start with an audit, fix the issues that block key tasks first (like contacting you or making a purchase), and then work through the rest. Train anyone who updates the site so new content stays accessible. Finally, consider publishing an accessibility statement that explains your commitment and gives visitors a way to report problems.
Accessibility is an ongoing habit, not a one-time project.

posts.title: CMS or Static Site? How to Choose the Right Foundation for Your Website
posts.intro: Before a single page is designed, every website project faces a quiet but important decision: how will this site be built and managed? The answer shapes how fast your site loads, how easily your team can update it, how much it costs to maintain, and how exposed it is to security problems. Most business websites end up on one of two paths, a content management system (CMS) or a static site, with a growing middle ground between them.
body: There is no universally right choice. There is only the right choice for how your business actually works. Here is how to think it through.

**A traditional CMS** such as WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla stores your content in a database. When someone visits a page, the server pulls content from the database, combines it with a template, and builds the page on the spot. You log in to an admin dashboard to edit text, add images, and publish posts.

**A static site** is made of pre-built HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. The pages are assembled ahead of time, often by a tool called a static site generator such as Hugo, Eleventy, Jekyll, or Astro, and then uploaded to a server or hosting platform. When a visitor arrives, the server simply hands over a finished file. There is no database lookup and no page building in real time.

**The middle ground** is a headless CMS. Services such as Contentful, Sanity, Strapi, or Decap CMS give editors a friendly interface for writing content, while the public website is generated as fast static pages. Editors get convenience; visitors get speed.
A database-driven CMS earns its popularity for good reasons:

ul: **Non-technical editing.** Staff can update pages, publish news, and swap images without touching code.
**Huge ecosystems.** Thousands of themes and plugins add features like events calendars, memberships, and online stores.
**Built-in workflows.** User roles, drafts, scheduled publishing, and revision history come standard or are easy to add.
**Dynamic features.** Search, user accounts, and personalized content are natural fits.

body: The trade-offs are real, though. A CMS needs regular updates to its core software, theme, and plugins. Each plugin is code written by someone else that you are trusting with your site. Pages can become slow if the hosting is weak or too many add-ons pile up. And because popular platforms are widely used, they are common targets for automated attacks.
Static sites have become a strong option for many small and mid-size businesses:

ul: **Speed.** Serving pre-built files is about as fast as the web gets, especially when combined with a content delivery network.
**Security.** With no database or server-side login on the public site, there are far fewer ways for an attacker to get in.
**Low maintenance.** There are no plugins to patch every month.
**Low hosting costs.** Many platforms host static sites inexpensively, and some offer free tiers for small sites.
**Version control.** Site files can live in a system like Git, so every change is tracked and easy to roll back.

body: The main limitation is editing. Without a CMS layer, updating content may mean editing files directly, which is fine for a developer but not for a busy office manager. Features that depend on real-time data, such as user logins, need extra services.

body.h2: Five Questions to Guide Your Decision

body: Rather than starting with technology, start with how your business operates. Your answers to these questions will usually point clearly in one direction.

ol: **Who will update the website, and how often?** If several non-technical staff publish content weekly, a CMS or headless CMS is worth it. If the site changes a few times a year, a static site may be ideal.

**What does the site need to do?** A brochure site, portfolio, or service business site fits a static approach well. Member areas, complex online stores, or heavy user interaction lean toward a CMS or a custom application.
**How important is speed?** Every approach can be fast with good engineering, but static sites make it easier by default.
**Who will handle maintenance?** If no one will reliably apply updates, a traditional CMS can become a liability. Be honest about this one.
**What is your total budget over time?** Compare not just the build cost but hosting, plugin licenses, security monitoring, and update work over three to five years.

body: To make this concrete, here is how the decision often plays out:

ul: **A local clinic or professional firm** with a handful of service pages and occasional updates: a static site, perhaps with a simple headless CMS for staff announcements.
**A restaurant or shop** that changes menus and promotions often: a CMS or headless CMS so staff can update quickly without calling a developer.
**A company publishing articles several times a week** with multiple authors and editors: a CMS with proper roles and workflow, or a headless setup with editorial features.
**A business needing bookings, accounts, or custom tools:** a CMS combined with dedicated services, or custom software built for the purpose.

body: These are starting points, not rules. Your specific needs, existing systems, and team skills all matter.
Whichever path you choose, a few habits protect your investment:

ul: Make sure you own your domain, hosting account, and content, and that you can export content if you ever move.
Keep the number of plugins or third-party services as small as practical.
Document how the site is built and updated, so you are not dependent on one person's memory.
Plan for backups and updates from day one, not after something breaks.

body: The best foundation is the one that fits your team's real habits and your customers' real needs, not the one with the most features on paper.

posts.title: Website Security Essentials: A Practical Checklist for Small Businesses
posts.intro: It is easy to assume that hackers only go after banks and large corporations. In reality, most attacks on websites are automated. Bots scan the internet around the clock looking for outdated software, weak passwords, and misconfigured servers. They do not care how big your company is; they care whether your site has an open door. A compromised website can show spam to your customers, redirect them to scam pages, leak form submissions, or be flagged by browsers as unsafe.
body: The encouraging news is that a handful of consistent habits prevent the large majority of everyday problems. Think of website security not as one big lock, but as several layers, each one making the next attack harder.

body.h2: Layer One: Encrypt Everything With HTTPS

body: HTTPS encrypts the connection between your visitor's browser and your website, so information like contact form entries and login details cannot be read or altered in transit. It relies on an SSL/TLS certificate installed on your server.
What to check:

ul: Every page on your site loads with `https://`, not just the checkout or contact page.
Visitors who type `http://` are automatically redirected to the secure version.
Your certificate renews automatically. Free certificates from Let's Encrypt, offered by many hosts, typically renew every 90 days, and an expired certificate triggers alarming browser warnings.
There is no "mixed content," meaning images or scripts still loading over plain HTTP.

body: Modern browsers label non-HTTPS pages as "Not secure," so this layer protects your reputation as much as your data.

body.h2: Layer Two: Keep Software Up to Date

body: Outdated software is one of the most common ways websites get compromised. When developers discover a security flaw in a CMS, plugin, or library, they release a fix. That same announcement also tells attackers exactly what to look for on sites that have not updated yet.
A sensible update routine looks like this:

ol: **Apply security updates promptly,** ideally within days of release, not months.
**Remove what you do not use.** Deactivated plugins and old themes can still be exploited if they remain installed.
**Choose maintained tools.** Before adding a plugin, check when it was last updated and whether it is actively supported.
**Test updates safely.** For important sites, apply updates to a staging copy first so a compatibility problem does not take your live site down.
**Do not forget the server.** The operating system, PHP or Node.js version, and database also need updating. On managed hosting, confirm your provider handles this.

body.h2: Layer Three: Control Who Gets In

body: Even perfectly updated software is vulnerable if someone can simply log in. Access control deserves real attention.

ul: **Use strong, unique passwords** for every account connected to your website: CMS admin, hosting, domain registrar, and email. A password manager makes this practical.
**Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA)** wherever it is offered. It is one of the most effective protections available, because a stolen password alone is no longer enough.
**Give people only the access they need.** A blog writer does not need administrator rights. Review user accounts periodically and remove former staff and contractors.
**Protect the login page.** Limiting repeated failed login attempts helps stop automated password guessing.
**Secure your domain registrar.** If someone takes over your domain account, they can redirect your website and email. Enable registrar lock and 2FA.

body.h2: Layer Four: Back Up as if You Will Need It

body: Backups are your safety net when everything else fails, whether the cause is an attack, a bad update, or simple human error. A backup you have never tested, however, is only a hope.

A widely used guideline is the **3-2-1 rule**: keep three copies of your data, on two different types of storage, with one copy stored off-site. For a website, that might mean your live site, your host's automatic backups, and a separate copy stored in a different cloud service.
Make sure your backups:

ul: Include both files and the database, if your site has one
Run automatically on a schedule that matches how often your content changes
Are kept for long enough to go back before a problem started, since some infections go unnoticed for weeks
Are restored as a test at least once or twice a year, so you know the process works

body.h2: Layer Five: Watch, Filter, and Plan

body: The final layer is about noticing problems early and responding calmly.

ul: **Uptime monitoring** alerts you when your site goes down. Many simple services offer this for free or at low cost.
**A web application firewall (WAF)**, available from many hosts and CDN providers, filters malicious traffic before it reaches your site.
**Google Search Console** notifies you if Google detects malware or hacked content on your site.
**Security headers** such as Content-Security-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security tell browsers to enforce safer behavior.
**Minimal data collection.** The less sensitive information your forms collect and store, the less there is to lose.

body: Finally, write down a short incident plan. Who do you call if the site is hacked? Where are the backups? Who has the hosting and domain logins? Answering these questions on a calm day saves hours of panic on a bad one.
Security works best as a routine. Here is a starting schedule you can adapt:

ul: **Weekly:** Apply available updates; glance at uptime and security alerts.
**Monthly:** Review user accounts; confirm backups are running; check that your certificate is valid.
**Quarterly:** Remove unused plugins and accounts; review third-party scripts; check Search Console for warnings.
**Twice a year:** Test a full backup restore; review your incident plan and contact list.

body: None of these tasks takes long on its own. Together, they make your website a far less appealing target.
